en: Okays appointment of Jumoke Gafar as board secretary/legal adviser Deji Elumoye in Abuja President Bola Tinubu has nominated six executive directors for the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA). Presidential spokesperson, Bayo Onanuga, in a release issued on Friday, disclosed that the president has forwarded a letter to the Senate for the confirmation of the six executive director-nominees. Three nominees are being reappointed, while three are new and once the Senate approves them, all nominees will serve a five-year term. The renominated executive directors are Mr Abiodun Adeniji, Executive Director, Finance and Accounts; Mr Ogbugo Kalu Ukoha, Executive Director, Distribution Systems, Storage and Retailing Infrastructure; and Dr Mustapha Lamorde, Executive Director, Health, Safety, Environment and Community. The new executive directors are: Mr Mobolaji Tajudeen Musa, Executive Director, Hydrocarbon Processing Plants, Installations and Transportation Infrastructure; Ms Ogechukwu Modie, Executive Director, Economic Regulations and Strategic Planning; and Mr Said Abutalib, Executive Director, Corporate Services and Administration. The president urged the Senate to consider the nominations expeditiously to ensure institutional continuity and strengthen the Authority’s oversight capacity. Tinubu also approved the appointment of Mrs Jumoke Gafar as Secretary to the Board/Authority and Legal Adviser, subject to completing the statutory processes under Section 46 of the PIA. In April, the president had appointed Rabiu Abdullahi Umar as the agency’s chief executive. 🇷🇺 Putin hosts 22 African heads of state in Moscow and tells them the West wants to push Africa "back into debt bondage," as Amnesty presses leaders over Africans recruited to fight in Ukraine

Vladimir Putin opened the third Russia-Africa summit in Moscow on Wednesday with a pitch aimed squarely at Washington and Brussels. Delegations from 48 African countries are attending, 22 of them led by heads of state, according to Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov. That is up from 17 heads of state in 2023, though well short of the 43 who came to Sochi in 2019. Kenya's William Ruto, Egypt's Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, Ethiopia's Abiy Ahmed, Rwanda's Paul Kagame and Sudan's army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan are among those listed, along with the Sahel juntas that have swapped French troops for Russian ones.

"The multipolar world is truly becoming a reality, and this trend is objective and irreversible," Putin told the plenary session, according to the Kremlin transcript. He accused unnamed Western countries of tariff wars, "illegitimate sanctions" and "active attempts" to drive Africans "back into debt bondage." He offered grain, fertilizer, nuclear power, hydropower and digital government systems, said Russia has "two of our own large language models" it is ready to share, and set a target of doubling Russia-Africa trade, which he put at over $27 billion last year, to more than $50 billion. He said Russia shipped 13 million tonnes of farm products to Africa in the first nine months of 2026. Leaders are due to adopt an action plan for 2027 to 2029 on Thursday.

The numbers carry a caveat. Al Jazeera notes Russia's trade with Africa is concentrated in a few countries and dwarfed by China's and the EU's, and that Moscow's real growth has been in security: Russian missions or troops now operate in at least nine African countries, according to the consultancy African Security Analysis. There is also a cost Putin did not mention. Amnesty International used the run-up to urge leaders to demand an end to what it calls deceptive and coercive recruitment of Africans to fight for Russia in Ukraine, an issue that has already strained ties with Kenya.

For Americans, the guest list is the point. Kenya is a major non-NATO ally of the United States, and Egypt is one of its largest aid recipients. Both sent their leaders to Moscow during a war Washington is trying to end on terms Russia keeps rejecting.
